title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired study (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating under shared_initial_candidate semantics. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator. All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Because the study used shared_initial_candidate semantics, the confirmatory contrast evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates and does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or model sampling variance. We present the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result (ceiling effects), and artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that avoid degeneracy.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows for NetOps. Operational deployment requires evidence that model outputs will not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied to live networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports stress that operational trustworthiness depends heavily on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures that pair generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited.  

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.  

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic Batfish‑style validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents under shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and no repair activity; (4) an interpretation of ceiling effects traceable to task bank, validator alignment, and generation semantics; and (5) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps work covers intent‑based configuration translation, runbook generation, log/RCA, and agentic automation proposals. Recent surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and recommend verifier‑coupled pipelines, RAG anchoring, and external safety checks [1]–[3]. Benchmarks for logs and retrieval identify performance and safety tradeoffs relevant to operational pipelines [5].  

Cross‑domain evidence and methodological gap. In adjacent domains (e.g., program repair and DevOps), generate→validate→repair pipelines have been proposed and applied; empirical reports document repair or safety benefits under specific datasets and validators, but these findings are dataset‑ and validator‑specific and do not generalize without adaptation [6],[4]. Two methodological gaps motivate our paired design: (i) when pipeline arms permit independent model draws, comparisons confound validator effects with model sampling variance; and (ii) many existing benchmarks emphasize QA or retrieval metrics but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators with paired protocols that preserve initial candidate sampling. Our shared_initial_candidate experiment isolates validator/repair/gate effects on identical initial generations and therefore directly addresses the first gap.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered (autocand_A1_prereg_v1). The preregistration fixed the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one sampled generation reused for both arms per intent), model/adaptor (gpt‑5‑mini via the registered adapter), deterministic validator and gate policy, repair budget (max 1 automated repair per intent), deterministic task selection (task_count = 200 paired intents), and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). These items were frozen prior to observing outputs and are archived in the run's execution bundle.  

Generation semantics clarification (preregistered and executed). The executed generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent. Consequently, the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on the same first‑pass candidate and does not measure any effect from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance.  

Model and validator configuration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini. Deterministic validator: a Batfish‑style validator implementing sequence ordering, interface precondition checks, final_group and minimum_up constraints, protected interfaces, and reachability/policy consistency. Model configuration recorded that max_output_tokens=2000 and maximum_attempts_per_call=1. Note: the archived model configuration records temperature=null for the executed calls; null/unset temperature is not evidence of deterministic model sampling (it does not imply temperature=0), and the adapter does not guarantee deterministic model sampling. The adapter produced exactly one sampled generation per pair that was reused under shared_initial_candidate semantics; no claim of deterministic sampling is made.  

Task bank and sampling. The deterministic task generator produced intent→configuration items with embedded constraints (allowed_fields, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, workflow_policies, and explicit required_sequence lists). The preregistered sampler selected 200 paired intents using a fixed index rule; selection was fixed and outcome‑independent. Difficulty labels in the manifest are concentrated in two levels: extreme = 40 tasks (20%), very_hard = 160 tasks (80%).  

Interventions, gating, and scoring. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate without gating. Guarded: feed the identical shared initial candidate to the deterministic validator; the deterministic gate followed a preregistered accept/reject rule and permitted up to one automated repair attempt when violations were detected. Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization. Per‑episode validator traces, repair flags, and scoring outputs were recorded in the archived execution bundle.  

Confirmatory analysis (frozen). The primary confirmatory analysis used the registered paired binary executor. The 2×2 paired contingency compares unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded across pairs. The analysis reports discordant pair counts n10 (guarded_only) and n01 (baseline_only), an exact two‑sided test, and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). The missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) and the preregistered retry rule for infrastructure errors were followed; no retriable infrastructure failures occurred.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed as preregistered and completed without scientific exclusions or retriable infrastructure failures. Planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs × 2 conditions); model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair). The provider audit recorded 200 completed hosted model calls.  

Primary confirmatory outcome. The paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0: every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by the deterministic validator in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. The exact two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] using bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. The zero‑width CI and p = 1.0 are direct consequences of complete concordance (no discordant pairs) under the registered estimand.  

Repair activity and diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; no automated repairs were invoked. Representative episodes exercise sequencing constraints (VLAN migration, uplink failover, MTU upgrades), protected interfaces, and group availability constraints; validator diagnostics reported parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count and violation_count = 0 for recorded representative items.  

Missingness, contamination, and reconciliation. All 200 pairs are complete under the preregistered missingness policy; there were zero failed or unscorable episodes and no contamination flags in the executed run.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 indicates that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family used, and the deterministic validator's ruleset, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied the validator constraints; consequently the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The run artifacts support three concrete contributors to this ceiling effect: (1) task‑bank alignment—synthetic intents closely matched the expected prompt schema, increasing the probability of syntactically correct outputs; (2) validator tightness—the validator encoded sequencing and precondition checks consistent with the generator's reference sequencing, so correct syntactic mappings passed readily; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model variance that might have produced discordant outcomes.  

Design recommendations (artifact‑supported). To measure verifier/gate value under nondegenerate conditions we recommend: (a) augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents to raise baseline unsafe rates; (b) executing a design that uses independent generation per condition (two independent model calls per pair) or multiple independent samples per condition to capture guarded‑conditioned regeneration and model sampling variance (this increases the model_call budget accordingly); (c) testing multiple model variants or sampling temperatures to reveal model variance effects (the archived model configuration can be adapted); (d) increasing the automated repair budget or enabling iterative repair loops to evaluate repair effectiveness when initial violations occur; and (e) including human‑in‑the‑loop arms to assess operator decisions in response to validator flags. These recommendations follow directly from the archived execution and manifest metadata and from the preregistration constraints.  

Operational caveats. This null result does not imply that deterministic validators lack value in more realistic or adversarial regimes; it demonstrates that design choices (task bank composition, generation semantics, validator rule set) determine whether a paired shared‑candidate contrast can detect verifier value. Field deployments require adversarial testing, independent per‑condition sampling, or HITL arms to quantify operational benefit and risk.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with a paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model, synthetic task bank, deterministic sampling semantics, and validator ruleset; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes (e.g., independent condition generation, adversarial inputs, multiple model samples) [1]–[4],[6]. We archive the full execution and analysis bundle and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions.

limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from identical initial candidates; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect approximately a 10 percentage‑point reduction but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank composition: difficulty labels in the executed bank were extreme = 40 (20%) and very_hard = 160 (80%); researchers seeking nondegenerate baselines should revise generation seeds or inject adversarial items.
